options.label: Rarefaction
options.summary: Repeated subsampling to a common depth. Discards reads and excludes shallow samples.

options.label: CSS scaling
options.summary: Cumulative sum scaling. Keeps every sample, assumes a shared scaling regime.

options.label: CLR transform
options.summary: Centered log-ratio. Compositionally rigorous, needs a zero-replacement rule.

note.message: Rarefaction is the selected default for this run (381/490 retained = 77.8%, above the 50% floor). This choice applies to alpha and beta diversity (Bray–Curtis, Jaccard, UniFrac). Raw unrarefied counts will be preserved and used for differential abundance in Step 7, where each DA method applies its own normalization. CLR/Aitchison will remain available as an optional compositional sensitivity analysis for beta diversity.

positions.claim: Rarefaction by repeated subsampling provides robust control of sequencing-depth effects on alpha and beta diversity metrics, removing dependence on differential sampling effort.
Rarefaction discards valid sequence reads and is statistically inadmissible for differential abundance testing, inflating variance to match the smallest library and reducing statistical power.

Sequencing data are compositional by construction, and the appropriate solution is log-ratio transformation (CLR/Aitchison geometry) applied consistently throughout the pipeline, not a preprocessing depth choice.

g1.exclusion_rationale: The nonCRC group (patients with colorectal disease but without cancer) is neither a clean control nor a clean case. The primary biological comparison in a CRC association study is healthy controls (H) vs. cancer cases (CRC). The nonCRC group can be explored in secondary or sensitivity analyses but should not be conflated with either pole of the main comparison.
g1.note_message: DiseaseState provides a clean three-level categorical outcome that aligns with standard CRC epidemiological framing (healthy, non-cancer disease, cancer). It is simpler and more directly interpretable than diagnosis_s, which conflates disease progression stages (adenoma → advanced adenoma → cancer) with risk stratification (High Risk Normal), making it ambiguous which subsets form the actual case and control arms. DiseaseState's structure (H: 172, CRC: 120, nonCRC: 198) is well-balanced and clearly labeled.

g2.note_message: No metadata column was classified as a technical/batch variable. The original study (Baxter et al. 2016) likely describes sample allocation to sequencing runs in its methods section, but a direct citation could not be retrieved at this time. The analysis will proceed assuming batch effects were either randomized or negligible, pending human verification against the published methods.

g3.note_message: All 490 samples are independent observations: there is no subject_id column in the metadata, repeated_subjects = 0, and n_subjects equals n_samples. Downstream inference should treat these as independent samples with no within-subject clustering or pairing.

recommendation.label: RECOMMENDS GENUS
recommendation.rationale: With 254 genus-level features, 92 family-level features, and 17 phylum-level features, genus represents the finest reliable resolution for short-read 16S while maintaining reasonable feature count and statistical power. Genus level avoids the information loss of coarser ranks and aligns with the standard interpretable resolution reported in published microbiome association studies.

note.message: With 381 independent samples distributed across five diagnosis groups (Normal 122, Cancer 120, adv Adenoma 109, Adenoma 89, High Risk Normal 50) and no pairing from G3, a standard significance threshold of α = 0.05 (two-sided) applies. The three primary alpha-diversity metrics—observed richness, Shannon, and Simpson—form a small, inherently correlated hypothesis family measuring complementary aspects of within-sample diversity (rare-taxon richness, abundance-weighted diversity, and common-taxon dominance). Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction is applied across these 3 alpha metrics only, keeping the raw p-values visible; this correction scope is explicitly separate from the hundreds of Step-7 differential-abundance tests, which form a distinct hypothesis family and must not be pooled into a single BH procedure. The 77.8% sample retention (381/490) post-rarefaction is reasonable; monitor for asymmetric losses by group during sensitivity analysis if richness is a primary endpoint.

Rarefication (not CLR) was selected in G6, so the default metric is Bray-Curtis (abundance-weighted). This pipeline operates on five independent diagnosis groups (Normal: 122, Cancer: 120, adv Adenoma: 109, Adenoma: 89, High Risk Normal: 50) with 70.8% sparsity. Jaccard (presence/absence) remains available as a sensitivity check. UniFrac is unavailable—no phylogenetic tree exists for this dataset.

Prevalence filter: 10% (102 genera retained). The step from 5% (124 genera) to 10% (102 genera) is a modest 18% reduction, indicating sparse features cluster near the 5–10% boundary. Moving to 20% removes only 22 additional taxa, suggesting minimal sensitivity loss beyond 10%. At this threshold each retained genus is detected in ~29+ samples overall, reducing the testing burden from 255 to 102 taxa while preserving detectably present organisms. DA method: Single transparent sensitivity analysis (CLR + Wilcoxon rank-sum), not a multi-method consensus, due to Python pipeline constraints.

synthesis.hero_finding: CRC-associated microbiota shows modest, statistically significant community compositional shift with robust enrichment of four CRC-linked pathogenic taxa (Porphyromonas, Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus) replicating cross-cohort literature signatures, but no community-wide diversity loss.
synthesis.summary_text: In 292 subjects (CRC: 120, H: 172) sequenced at genus level, colorectal cancer cases showed a measurable but small community-level signature: no global loss of within-sample richness or evenness (Shannon p=0.75, Simpson p=0.79), but significantly lower observed taxon count (p=0.0019) and estimated richness (Chao1 p=0.0039). Between-sample composition differed significantly (PERMANOVA R²=0.0062, p=0.046), though the effect explained minimal variance and significant unequal dispersion was detected (p=0.003, confounding potential). At the taxon level, 11 of 102 genera met significance after FDR correction. CRC enrichment concentrated in four well-established pathogenic anaerobes—Porphyromonas (q=0.00015, LFC −1.79), Fusobacterium (q=0.0086, LFC −0.93), Parvimonas (q=0.034, LFC −0.61), Peptostreptococcus (q=0.041, LFC −1.09)—all directionally concordant with independent CRC cohort literature. In contrast, butyrate-producing protective taxa (Roseburia, Faecalibacterium) showed no significant depletion despite literature expectation, remaining near-universal (Roseburia q=0.48, Faecalibacterium q=0.47).
synthesis.literature_validation_text: Four of five CRC-enriched genera replicate prior cross-cohort metagenomic signatures (Porphyromonas, Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus directionally confirmed via Thomas et al. 2019), representing genuine replication rather than novel discovery. Notably, two prominent butyrate producers expected to be depleted in CRC (Roseburia, Faecalibacterium; Duvallet et al. 2017 meta-analysis) showed no significant difference in this cohort (q>0.47), despite their theoretical protective role and widespread prior evidence of depletion. This discordance may reflect cohort-specific factors, disease stage heterogeneity, or confounding by medication/diet not captured at genus resolution.

limitations.title: Genus-level resolution
limitations.body: 16S rRNA genus-level classification cannot discriminate species or strain variants within taxa such as Fusobacterium (e.g., F. nucleatum subspecies with different virulence profiles) or Porphyromonas, potentially masking species-specific associations or opposing effects within a single genus.

limitations.title: Cross-sectional design and causality
limitations.body: This study is a cross-sectional case–control comparison and cannot establish causal relationships; CRC-enriched taxa may be consequences of disease-related alterations (diet, antimotility, bile acid shifts, immune changes) rather than drivers of pathology.

limitations.title: Sequencing depth imbalance residual confound
limitations.body: 109 samples were excluded due to insufficient sequencing depth for rarefaction at 4,200 reads/sample, creating a cohort that is biased toward deeper libraries. If excluded samples were non-randomly distributed between cases and controls, this exclusion could systematically distort group comparisons.

limitations.title: Unequal dispersion and small effect size
limitations.body: PERMANOVA detected significant unequal sample-to-sample dispersion between groups (p=0.003), meaning cases and controls differ not only in central tendency but in variability. Combined with the small R² (0.0062), community-level differences may not be biologically meaningful or reproducible, and may partly reflect batch/technical factors.

limitations.title: Confounding variables not examined
limitations.body: Age, sex, medication (particularly antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs), diet, and geographic/batch effects are not stratified or adjusted in this genus-level analysis. Any of these could explain or exaggerate the observed taxon-level signals, particularly the unexpected absence of butyrate-producer depletion.

next_steps.title: Test Fusobacterium specificity in CDI
next_steps.hypothesis: Porphyromonas and Fusobacterium enrichment in CRC represents a CRC-specific signature rather than a generic marker of intestinal dysbiosis.
next_steps.experiment: Reanalyze the C. difficile infection (CDI) cohort (cdi_schubert) available within this project using identical preprocessing and DA methods. Compare the direction and effect size of Porphyromonas and Fusobacterium enrichment in CDI versus this CRC dataset. If both conditions show similar enrichment, the signal is a generic dysbiosis marker; if CDI shows no enrichment or opposite direction, CRC-specificity is supported.

next_steps.title: Resolve Fusobacterium nucleatum subspecies via shotgun metagenomics
next_steps.hypothesis: CRC-enriched Fusobacterium represents virulent subspecies (e.g., F. nucleatum subsp. animalis or polymorphum) carrying CRC-associated virulence factors like FadA, not merely background commensals.
next_steps.experiment: Perform whole-genome shotgun metagenomics on a stratified subset of CRC (n≥20) and healthy control (n≥20) samples with high and low Fusobacterium 16S abundance. Assemble and classify Fusobacterium species and subspecies, measure FadA virulence factor carriage, and quantify subspecies-level abundance difference between cases and controls. If CRC cases are dominated by FadA-positive polymorphum while controls carry only F. nucleatum subsp. nucleatum, the mechanistic hypothesis of virulence factor-mediated pathology gains credibility.

next_steps.title: Investigate butyrate-producer absence via stratification
next_steps.hypothesis: Roseburia and Faecalibacterium are depleted in a CRC subgroup defined by disease stage, medication exposure, or pre-existing dysbiosis severity, but remain normal in early-stage or medication-naive cases, explaining the null result.
next_steps.experiment: Stratify the CRC cohort by disease stage (if available in metadata), antibiotic/PPI use in the prior 6 months, and baseline Shannon diversity quartile. Within each stratum, repeat Wilcoxon rank-sum testing for Roseburia and Faecalibacterium abundance. If depletion emerges in a defined subgroup (e.g., antibiotic-exposed or advanced-stage cases) but not overall, this resolves the literature discordance and suggests a confounded signal in the full cohort.

next_steps.title: Quantify dispersion-driven bias in PERMANOVA
next_steps.hypothesis: The significant PERMANOVA result (p=0.046) is inflated by unequal dispersion (p=0.003) and does not represent a true between-group compositional shift; resampling or robust permutation approaches will weaken the signal.
next_steps.experiment: Rerun PERMANOVA using dispersion-adjusted methods (e.g., distance-to-centroid analysis or permutation under reduced model controlling for variance heterogeneity). Calculate 95% confidence intervals around the R² estimate via bootstrap. If adjusted R² drops below 0.004 or the CI crosses zero, the original p-value is not reliable and community-level differences are not robust.
